newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senators seek permanent trade ties with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators seek permanent trade ties with China.

text.p: Two senior members of the influential Senate Finance Committee introduced legislation on Tuesday to grant China permanent trading privileges with the United States.

Sens. Max Baucus, D.-Mt., and John Chafee, R.-R.I., said they would start pushing for the legislation that would end the annual ritual of reviewing China's trade status once Beijing made an acceptable offer to join the World Trade Organisation.

"We are waiting for China to come up with a commercially acceptable WTO offer," Baucus told a news conference. "If China won't do it, the bill will not go much further. But if they do, then we will push it as hard as we can."
The bill, he said, would give the president authority to grant permanent Most Favoured Nation trade status with China.
President Clinton has until June 3 to decide whether to renew China's MFN status. Congress can then vote to accept it or reject MFN.

Administration officials have already made clear that Clinton will renew the trade status that allows Chinese goods into the United States at the low tariff rates enjoyed by almost every other country. Only six countries do not have MFN status with the United States.

Administration officials are gearing up for a tough battle over China's trading status this year. Concerns about human rights, nuclear technology sales and the huge U.S. trade deficit with China are factors in the debate.
The handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1 and allegations that Beijing may have tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal contributions also are weighing on lawmakers.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Sunday he thought there would be less support this year for MFN renewal than last year when the House voted 286 to 141 to back Clinton's renewal of China's trade status.

Some lawmakers have suggested linking renewal to a three- or six-month review of Beijing's handling on the takeover of Hong Kong. But Hong Kong officials have objected to that, arguing that revoking MFN would be as commercially disastrous for Hong Kong as it would for China.
Baucus said that giving permanent MFN for China would help stablize relations and that revoking the trade privilege would do nothing to advance the cause of human rights.

"It would cause immense human suffering by putting millions of Chinese out of work," he said. "And because of that, it would also turn the Chinese public against our human rights policy generally. So we can only expect to accomplish anying on human rights by keeping MFN in place."
